story_title: The Potatoes That Wait for Frost

teller.name: Bram Hollis
teller.who: carpenter who grew up in the old mill house beside the pond

listener: a late walker invited in to sit by the little stove in the mill house on Old Mill Pond
summary: On the night of the first hard frost, the old miller lays small potatoes on the slate ledge by the pond, an Andean way of letting the cold do the work. His friend in the mountains taught him by letter.
source_tradition: Quechua and Aymara communities of the Andes (chuño, freeze-dried potatoes)
source_note: Chuño is a long-documented traditional food practice of Andean highland communities; the miller, the pond, the pen friend and the story are original.
hook: Why does Percival Oake lay a tray of small potatoes out on the mill pond ledge on the coldest night of the year, and who are they for?
context: Percival Oake is the retired miller of Old Mill Pond; tonight, with the first hard frost promised, he uses a method taught by a mountain pen friend.

description_summary: A carpenter tells how the old miller lays small potatoes on a slate ledge for the first frost, a custom learned by letter from a friend in the Andes.
description_setting: Mid October in Fernwick, a clear cold night at Old Mill Pond. A lantern glows beside a still wheel, a little stove ticks, and tea and toast are shared while the frost gathers.
image_brief: A still black mill pond at night beside a stone mill house, a lantern hanging by a window casting a warm yellow circle on a slate ledge holding a tray of small purple and cream potatoes on sacking, a slow wheel against a starry sky, fine frost starting on the stone. No faces, no text, no religious symbols.
new_world_facts: Percival Oake, the old miller, lives in the mill house on Old Mill Pond (green door that sticks, split brown knuckles); each year on the first hard frost he lays small potatoes on the slate ledge, an Andean custom taught by letter by his pen friend Marisol.
Bram Hollis, a carpenter, grew up in the mill house; the stove there has a dented kettle.
On the longest night of winter Percival makes a pot of soup for whoever knocks.
The mill has been still for many years but the wheel creaks in the night air.

script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Potatoes That Wait for Frost, told by Bram Hollis, a carpenter who grew up in the old mill house beside the pond. Settle in somewhere warm, and I will do the talking.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Tray on the Ledge]]

Mind the step, the stone is worn in the middle. Come in and sit by the stove, the little one with the dented kettle. There. Now, you will have noticed what is on the ledge outside the window, because everyone does. Why does Percival Oake lay a tray of small potatoes out on the mill pond ledge on the coldest night of the year, and who are they for? I wondered it for years, long before I ever asked him, and I will tell you how the answer came.

[pause]

Percival is the old miller, though the mill has been still for longer than I have been a carpenter. He has big hands, split and brown at the knuckles, and a slow way of nodding as if every question deserved a minute. He lives in the mill house on Old Mill Pond, behind Fernwick, with a green door that sticks in damp weather and a roof that holds the smell of a hundred years of flour.

[pause]

Inside, the kitchen is low and brown and crowded. Copper pans hang from a beam in order of size. A rag rug lies in front of the stove, worn thin where boots have stood. The table is scarred pine, scrubbed pale, with a blue jug of dried grasses in the middle of it. There is an old sack-hoist in the corner that nobody has used since before I was born, and Percival hangs his hat on it. The room smells of woodsmoke, damp wool, and the dusty sweetness of the wheat that is still, somehow, in the walls.

[pause]

The pond is quiet tonight. It lies flat and black, with a few last frogs murmuring in the rushes, and the mill wheel stands against the sky with a faint, slow creak as the night air moves it. It is the middle of October, clear and cold, and the first hard frost of the year has been promised. You can taste it already, a clean, metal thinness in the air, with a trace of apple and leaf smoke in it.

[long pause]

Along the far bank, the willows hang their long thin leaves into the water, yellowing now, and a few have drifted onto the surface and turned slowly, like tiny boats. The sky above the wheel is the color of dark slate, and the stars come out one at a time, pale and sharp. Somewhere a gate clicks shut. Somewhere an owl asks its one question, and is not answered.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER A Letter from the Mountains]]

The potatoes came in a cloth bag, in a parcel, from very far away. Years ago, Percival had a pen friend, a woman named Marisol, who lived high in the Andes mountains, in a village so far up that the clouds sit below it in the mornings. They wrote to each other about weather, mostly. He wrote about rain on the pond. She wrote about wind on the high grass, and llamas, and the color of the sky at that height, which she said was the deepest blue you can imagine.

[pause]

She described her village in one of those letters, and I have read it so many times that I can see it. Low houses of stone and earth, with thatch the color of straw. Terraces stepping up the hillside like the rungs of a ladder. Women in layered skirts and wide-brimmed hats, carrying bundles on their backs wrapped in bright striped cloth. In the morning, she wrote, the ground is white and crisp and rings under your boots, and the whole valley smells of cold stone and woodsmoke and boiling corn.

[pause]

One autumn, her letter was thicker than usual. Inside was a small bag of knobbly potatoes, as small as walnuts, purple and yellow and cream. And a page of careful writing, in two languages. It told him about something her family has done for longer than anyone remembers. People in those cold mountain villages, the Quechua and Aymara people, make a food called chuño. They do it with the weather itself.

[pause]

This is how it goes. On the clearest nights of the dry season, when the frost comes down hard, the potatoes are spread on the cold ground under the stars. They freeze solid till morning. The next day the sun warms them a little, and the families tread on them with bare feet to squeeze out the water. Then back they go to the frost, and back under the sun, for several days. In the end the potatoes are light and wrinkled and dry as small stones, and they keep for years. In a land where the weather is harsh, a bag of chuño is a pantry that never goes bad.

[long pause]

There is a quiet kind of cleverness in it, I think. Nobody invented a machine. Nobody burned anything. They looked at the cold, which might have been a trouble, and they asked what it was good for. The frost, the dry air, the long clear nights, and the thin bright sun of the following day each have their own small job, like members of a very slow team. The people who first worked it out are lost to us. But the potatoes remember, every one of them.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Waiting for the Cold]]

Percival read that letter standing at the stove, with his tea going cold beside him. And he thought it the loveliest bit of sense he had ever heard. A craft of waiting. A food made not by fire, but by the right night.

[pause]

So he tried it here, with Marisol's potatoes, in a clear week in October. Of course the Fernwick frost is a soft frost, and not a mountain one. But the ledge by the pond is made of old slate, and slate gives up its warmth quickly, and on the stillest nights it grows a fine white fur of ice. He lays the potatoes out in a single layer on a tray lined with clean sacking. He takes his time. One potato, then another, never touching, like beads on a string.

[pause]

I watched him do it tonight, as I have many nights. The lantern hangs from the hook by the window and makes a warm yellow circle on the slate. His boots scuff softly. The sacking is rough and smells of dry earth and straw. The potatoes are cool to the touch and a little dusty, purple and cream in the lamplight. He sets the last one down, and steps back, and looks at the tray with his head on one side.

[long pause]

"That's all," he says. "Now it's up to the night."

[pause]

[[CHAPTER Tea by the Stove]]

Then we come inside, and he pours the tea. The kettle gives a low whistle and settles. The stove ticks as it warms, and a log shifts and sighs into red ash. On the shelf there is a loaf, which he cuts with a worn serrated bread saw into thick, uneven slices, and we toast them on a long fork at the open stove door till the edges go gold. We eat them with honey. The crust crackles, the honey runs, and for a while neither of us says anything.

[pause]

I asked him at last, years back, who the potatoes were for. He thought about it, turning his cup. "Well," he said, "the first year, they were for Marisol. To say thank you, in a way. Then they were for me, to have something to wait for. And now I make a pot of soup on the longest night of winter, and it is for whoever knocks." He smiled at his cup. "They always knock."

[long pause]

I have been at that soup, you know. It is brown and thick and plain, with the dry, wrinkled potatoes soaked soft overnight, and an onion, and a handful of herbs from the sill, and a little salt. It tastes of earth, and a faint sweetness, and the long patient cold. The whole town fits into that kitchen somehow, on coats and on stools and on the floor, with bowls steaming in their hands, and the windows run with warm mist, and the wheel stands outside in the snow. Nobody counts. There is always enough.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Morning Will Do the Rest]]

I stay a while longer by the stove tonight. The window has grown a faint feathery pattern of frost at its corners. Out on the ledge, the potatoes are quiet in their rows. Tomorrow the sun will warm the slate, and Percival will tread them gently in a wooden trough, in thick woolen socks, humming something off tune.

[pause]

But tonight the work is the cold's. That is the part I like best. There is nothing for anyone to do. The pond lies still, and the wheel creaks once, and the stove ticks. The frogs have gone almost silent. A long way up in the mountains, I like to think, someone else is laying a tray under the same stars, and the two trays are saying the same quiet thing to the night.

[long pause]

Percival's head is nodding now. His cup sits empty in his big brown hands. I lift the old gray blanket from the chair back and tuck it over his knees. He does not wake. The lamp burns low on its hook, and I leave it so.

[long pause]

Frost is coming to the ledge. The potatoes will wait for it. There is no hurry in any of it, none at all.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Why does Percival Oake lay potatoes on the ledge at night? Because a friend in the mountains taught him to let the frost do the work.

[pause]

He sets them in a row on sacking. One, and another, and another. The lantern glows. The pond is still.

[long pause]

The cold comes down. The potatoes freeze. In the morning the sun will warm them, and he will tread them softly, and they will dry, and keep.

[pause]

He drinks his tea. His eyes grow heavy. The stove ticks low.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the potatoes that wait for frost. The stove is warm, and the chair is yours, and the night will do the rest. Good night.
